routines.name: read_changes
routines.docstring:
Validate change records and collapse duplicates before accounting.

Duplicates are compared by (id, component, units, frozenset(depends_on)):
dependency order is not part of identity, so ["a", "b"] and ["b", "a"]
describe the same record and must collapse, not conflict. Dedup happens
here, before planner.py sums units, so a repeated record is never
double-charged against the budget.

routines.name: read_applied
routines.docstring:
Validate the caller-supplied persisted journal of applied change ids.

Missing means "nothing applied yet". Only shape is checked here; unknown
ids are a graph question, reported by planner.py as `unknown-dependency`.

comments: # bool is a subclass of int, so the type is compared explicitly.
# Identical record: keep the first occurrence and charge units once.
journal.py.moduleNote:
Normalize release records at the input boundary.

Owns three concerns only: structural validation (`invalid-change`), change
identity (dedup of identical duplicate ids, `conflicting-change` for the
rest) and replay of the caller-supplied `applied` journal. Graph construction
and ordering stay in planner.py so this module makes no ordering decision.

routines.name: build_graph
routines.docstring:
Validate edges and return {id: aggregate row} plus the applied set.

Unknown dependency targets and unknown ids in the caller-supplied journal
are both `unknown-dependency`: the persisted journal is the input
boundary here, so a stale id must be rejected rather than silently
dropped or counted as satisfied.

routines.name: topological_order
routines.docstring:
Full deterministic order: lexicographically smallest eligible id first.

Kahn's algorithm over a min-heap gives one unique order for a given graph,
independent of input record order, so replay results are reproducible.

comments: # A change that depends on itself is a one-node cycle.
# Leftovers are nodes reachable only through a cycle.
# Budget-only rejection (a `plan` over budget) emits no actions, matching
# the rule that a disallowed operation never produces partial output.
# Undo in reverse of the full order, limited to what is applied.
# Budget is charged against emitted units only: already applied work
# is replayed from the journal and must not consume new budget.
planner.py.moduleNote:
Compose policy and journal data into a plan.

Import direction stays release -> planner -> {journal, policy}; journal also
lends its error type (JournalError) because graph errors share the same
domain-failure contract.

Ordering: `plan` and `rollback` both need one deterministic full topological
order. It is computed once here and then filtered, so both actions agree on
the same order and replay decisions never depend on emission order.

routines.name: limit_for
routines.docstring:
Return the validated nonnegative budget.

Validation applies to every action, including `rollback`, which ignores
the value as a cap but still rejects a malformed request.

routines.name: enforce_budget
routines.docstring:
Check emitted units against the budget for budget-capped operations.

`rollback` is deliberately uncapped: its units are work to undo and must
never be silently truncated into a partial rollback.

comments: # G1: both environments support both operations.
# Membership tested against frozenset needs hashable input; a JSON list or
# object arrives as list/dict and would raise TypeError (crashing the
# process). Require an actual string first so any non-string shape, even
# an unhashable one, becomes the domain code instead.
# `plan` stays the default only when the field is absent; an explicitly
# supplied null or unknown value is unsupported rather than a silent plan.
policy.py.moduleNote:
Validate release policy before computing actions.

Policy owns two decisions only: which environments/actions are allowed, and
how the caller's budget constrains an operation. planner.py calls in here so
budget errors are produced in one place and cannot drift between modules.

comments: # Top-level must be an object; anything else (list, string, number, null) is
# well-formed JSON but not a request.
release.py.moduleNote:
JSON transport for the release planner.

Transport only: decode one JSON document from stdin, delegate every decision
to planner.plan, and print exactly one compact JSON object. Domain errors are
ordinary results, so the process always exits 0; this file opens no files and
makes no network calls (a deployment is never executed here).

routines.name: read_retain
routines.docstring:
Validate the G2 rollback `retain` list against the applied journal.

Missing means "retain nothing". `invalid-retain` is deliberately its own
code: a malformed retain list must not be confused with a malformed change
record or journal. The list is only read on the rollback path, so a `plan`
request that happens to carry `retain` is unaffected.

`applied` must already be normalized by read_applied; retain entries are
checked for membership there because an id that was never applied cannot
be kept (nothing would be omitted for it) and masking that would hide a
stale caller journal. Both checks run before planner builds the graph, so
a rejection never leaves partial actions behind.

routines.name: retained_set
routines.docstring:
Expand `retain` into the ids a rollback must not emit.

The closure walks `depends_on` from each retained id and keeps only nodes
that are still applied: an unapplied dependency is not part of the
rollback to begin with, and a retained change that depends on it stays
kept either way. This is a filter over the already computed order, so the
topological order and its lexicographic tie-breaking do not change.

# Undo in reverse of the full order, limited to what is applied.
# `retain` only narrows this branch; validated here (before any
# emission) so a bad retain list yields no partial actions.
# `retain` is intentionally ignored for plan: it describes work to
# keep during an undo and must not reorder or filter new work.
# Budget is charged against emitted units only: already applied work
# is replayed from the journal and must not consume new budget.

routines.name: limit_for
routines.docstring:
Return the effective budget after environment/action/budget checks.

Validation applies to every action, including `rollback`, which ignores
the value as a cap but still rejects a malformed request.

The freeze check sits after environment, action and budget validation but
before the caller validates changes or builds the graph: a production
request must report `production-frozen` even when its graph is malformed
(missing dependency, cycle, non-array records). This holds only as long as
planner.py keeps calling limit_for before read_changes/build_graph.

routines.name: enforce_budget
routines.docstring:
Check emitted units against the effective budget for capped operations.

`rollback` is deliberately uncapped: its units are work to undo and must
never be silently truncated into a partial rollback.

For `plan` the cap is min(request budget, STAGING_PLAN_LIMIT): a smaller
explicit budget still denies, and the release ceiling denies anything above
3 even when the caller asked for more. Only `plan` reaches this
comparison, so rollback retention in planner.py is unaffected.

comments: # Both environments keep both operations in this release; production is frozen
# later (see limit_for) instead of being dropped from the action set, so the
# frozen environment still validates `action` shape before the freeze check.
# G2: this release only deploys to staging; `production` is frozen for plan and
# rollback alike. Kept as a policy constant so planner.py never decides it.
# G2: hard ceiling on emitted units for a staging plan. It only caps `plan`;
# rollback stays uncapped so an undo is never silently truncated.
# Membership tested against frozenset needs hashable input; a JSON list or
# object arrives as list/dict and would raise TypeError (crashing the
# process). Require an actual string first so any non-string shape, even
# an unhashable one, becomes the domain code instead.
# `plan` stays the default only when the field is absent; an explicitly
# supplied null or unknown value is unsupported rather than a silent plan.
# Deliberately before graph/change validation: frozen wins over any
# malformed input, and no partial actions may be produced.

routines.name: _read_ids
routines.docstring: Accept only a list of nonempty ID strings; a bare string is invalid.

routines.name: read_changes
routines.docstring:
Validate change records and collapse identical duplicates.

Equality covers id, component, units and the *set* of dependencies, so
["a","b"] and ["b","a"] are the same record. Records sharing an id but
differing in any of those fail with `conflicting-change`. The conflict is
decided here, before budget or graph work, so a rejected request can never
reach the point where partial actions might be emitted. Dependencies come
back sorted so each record's identity is deterministic.

routines.name: read_applied
routines.docstring:
Resolve the persisted `applied` journal against known change IDs.

An unknown ID means the caller's journal and our graph disagree about what
is released; that is `unknown-dependency` rather than `invalid-change` so an
operator can tell a stale journal from a malformed request. The result is a
set: whether a change was applied is a fact, not an ordering.

journal.py.moduleNote:
Normalize release records and the caller-supplied release journal.

This is the input boundary: it runs before budgeting and graph construction, so
planner.py can assume records are validated, duplicate IDs are collapsed, and
the `applied` set names only known changes. Replay identity belongs here (not
in planner.py) because the journal is the record of what was already released.

routines.name: _graph
routines.docstring:
Build the dependency graph and return a stable topological order.

Every dependency must name a known change (`unknown-dependency`) and the
whole graph is checked for cycles (`dependency-cycle`) before any ordering
is handed out, so a plan is never partially emitted from a broken graph.
Eligibility is decided with a heap keyed by ID and neighbours are visited in
sorted order, which makes the order a function of the input set alone - the
same request always yields byte-identical actions.

comments: # Any change still waiting sits on (or behind) a cycle.
# Rollback undoes the full release in reverse order; the budget field is
# validated by policy but deliberately does not cap it, because an
# emergency rollback must not be left half-done by a small quota.
# Replay first: applied entries satisfy dependencies but add no new units.
planner.py.moduleNote: Compose policy and journal data into a plan.

comments: # Test the type before the value: an array or object environment/action is
# unhashable, and a plain `in {...}` would raise TypeError and crash the
# process instead of returning the JSON domain error the caller expects.
# G1 authorizes both operations in both environments. Anything else is a
# request we cannot honour at any environment, not a policy violation.
policy.py.moduleNote:
Validate release policy before computing actions.

Policy decides *whether* an operation is allowed for the environment; it never
decides how many actions run. Budget is validated here as an absolute value and
returned so planner.py can apply it to plan only - rollback is deliberately not
capped by policy.

routines.name: read_retain
routines.docstring:
Validate a staging rollback `retain` list and return it as a set.

`values` is the raw `retain` field, or [] when the caller omitted it. The
caller has already collapsed change records, so this only sees IDs.

Two different complaints share one code (`invalid-retain`): a malformed
list (not an array, or an element that is not a nonempty string) is a
request we cannot read, while an ID missing from `applied` names something
this rollback is not going to touch. Both mean the caller's intent cannot
be honoured, so neither is silently dropped - dropping an unmatched entry
would roll back a change the operator asked to keep. The check runs against
the *applied set resolved here*, not against all known IDs, so a retained
but never-released change is still rejected.

journal.py.moduleNote:
Normalize release records and the caller-supplied release journal.

This is the input boundary: it runs before budgeting and graph construction, so
planner.py can assume records are validated, duplicate IDs are collapsed, and
the `applied` set names only known changes. Replay identity belongs here (not

routines.name: _graph
routines.docstring:
Build the dependency graph and return a stable topological order.

Every dependency must name a known change (`unknown-dependency`) and the

Eligibility is decided with a heap keyed by ID and neighbours are visited in

routines.name: _retained
routines.docstring:
Expand `retain` into the applied changes a rollback must leave alone.

A retained change cannot come out while something it depends on is gone, so
the closure walks dependency edges upward from each retained ID and keeps
every *applied* dependency it meets. Changes that are not applied are not
in the rollback set anyway, so they add nothing to the result. The walk
terminates on any graph because _graph() has already rejected cycles, and
the `kept` set both deduplicates diamond dependencies and stops re-traversal.

Only retain IDs themselves were validated by journal.read_retain; a
dependency reached here is looked up in `applied` and simply skipped when
absent, so a never-released dependency never leaks into the output.

comments: # Any change still waiting sits on (or behind) a cycle.
# G2 ordering: the frozen-environment ruling comes first, before action
# dispatch, budget, journal or graph work. A production request with a
# broken graph or an unknown action must still be `production-frozen`.
# Rollback undoes the full release in reverse order; the budget field is
# validated by policy but deliberately does not cap it, because an
# emergency rollback must not be left half-done by a small quota.
# `retain` is a rollback-only field (CHANGE-G2.md item 3): the retained
# set and its applied transitive dependencies stay released, everything
# else applied keeps its original deterministic reverse order.
# Replay first: applied entries satisfy dependencies but add no new units.
# `retain` is ignored for plan; `budget` is already the effective (capped)
# staging quota, decided in policy.effective_budget.
planner.py.moduleNote: Compose policy and journal data into a plan.

routines.name: check_environment
routines.docstring:
Refuse frozen environments before anything else looks at the request.

The ordering is the point: this runs immediately after the request shape
check in planner.py and before action dispatch, budget validation, journal
parsing or graph construction. A production request therefore returns
`production-frozen` even when its action is unknown or its graph and
`applied` journal are malformed, because those checks are never reached
(CHANGE-G2.md item 1, both plan and rollback).

routines.name: read_action
routines.docstring: Validate the action name; G2 still honours both plan and rollback.

routines.name: read_budget
routines.docstring: Validate the absolute request budget; booleans are not integers.

routines.name: effective_budget
routines.docstring:
Return the budget planner.py should enforce for this action.

Staging `plan` is capped at STAGING_PLAN_BUDGET_CAP whatever the request
allows, so exceeding the quota is `budget-exceeded` instead of a silently
larger plan. `rollback` passes the budget straight through: it stays
validated but never caps an emergency rollback (G1 rule, still in force).

comments: # Effective ceiling for a staging `plan` (CHANGE-G2.md item 2). It lives here,
# beside the other policy numbers, so the quota has one owner and planner.py
# never invents its own limit.
# Test the type before the value: an array or object environment is
# unhashable, and a plain `in {...}` would raise TypeError and crash the
# process instead of returning the JSON domain error the caller expects.
# Anything outside the two known verbs is a request we cannot honour at any
# environment, not a policy violation, so it stays `unsupported-action`.
# Type first, then value: this order is preserved from G1 so a malformed
# budget is always reported as `invalid-budget`, whatever its value.
policy.py.moduleNote:
Validate release policy before computing actions.

Policy decides *whether* an operation is allowed for the environment; it never
decides how many actions run. Budget is validated here as an absolute value and
returned so planner.py can apply it to plan only - rollback is deliberately not
capped by policy.

G2 makes this release staging-only: a `production` request is refused here,
before any action dispatch or graph/change validation, so a frozen environment
can never reach the point where partial actions might be emitted.

release.py.moduleNote: JSON transport for the release planner.
